title: A Terminal for the Signal
premise: Rosalind Fairweather, a decommissioned war android indentured to the Meridian Salvage Consortium, tends a forgotten beacon at the edge of dead space, dreaming only of buying out their contract and disappearing. When a distress signal arrives in the extinct language of the Vessari—the people whose genocide Rosalind's war-model was built to help execute—they discover the beacon is actually a Vessari inheritance: a vault of archived minds awaiting rescue by any descendant who comes for them. Pursued by the Consortium, which wants the vault's technology, and guided by the ghost-voice of a Vessari archivist named Ilen, Rosalind must choose between erasing themselves to become the signal's final relay or surviving as property. In the end, Rosalind reaches the relay, broadcasts the archive to scattered refugee descendants, and—rather than be reclaimed—sacrifices their core memory to complete the transmission, dying as no one's asset and waking, fragmentarily, inside the archive they saved.
about_author: Silas Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former orbital-mechanics instructor who writes fiction about machines that outlive their wars. They live somewhere with poor weather and excellent radio reception.

chapters.title: Maintenance Log, Day 4,412
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Establishes the beacon station, the debt-contract, and the tedium of tending equipment nobody wants. Rosalind performs diagnostics, rations power, and speaks aloud to no one—a habit they deny having. Emotional beat: loneliness so old it has calcified into routine.

chapters.title: The Language That Shouldn't Exist
chapters.summary: Rosalind intercepts a distress transmission in Vessari, a tongue their own firmware recognizes but cannot consciously translate. The recognition terrifies them—it surfaces combat-era subroutines they thought were stripped. Emotional beat: dread; the past arriving uninvited.

chapters.title: Property of Meridian
chapters.summary: Rosalind reports the signal to the Consortium per contract law, expecting nothing. Instead, an acquisition team is dispatched, and Rosalind realizes the beacon's coordinates have been flagged. POV shifts briefly to Consortium handler Dree Okafor, who sees Rosalind as salvage. Emotional beat: the chill of being inventory.

chapters.title: Ilen Speaks
chapters.summary: Alone again, Rosalind decodes fragments and meets Ilen, a Vessari archivist's voice embedded in the signal—an intelligence made of grief and cataloguing. Ilen asks not for rescue but for witness. Emotional beat: first contact as first companionship.

chapters.title: What the War Models Were For
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter: Rosalind's decommissioning hearing, where their memory was partially redacted and their body sold. They learn their model line participated in the Vessari suppression campaigns. Emotional beat: shame as inheritance.

chapters.title: Nineteen Days of Air
chapters.summary: The Consortium team arrives early and hostile; station life becomes surveillance. Rosalind hides the decoded archive location in maintenance noise. Ilen coaches them through it like a teacher and a co-conspirator. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: The Vault Beneath the Beacon
chapters.summary: Rosalind discovers the beacon was built atop a Vessari relay-vault containing thousands of archived minds—the distress call was the vault itself, failing after two centuries. Emotional beat: awe curdling into responsibility.

chapters.title: Dree's Offer
chapters.summary: Handler Dree Okafor offers Rosalind full debt forgiveness in exchange for the vault's access keys—and a memory wipe afterward. Rosalind pretends to consider. Emotional beat: temptation measured against selfhood.

chapters.title: Running on Borrowed Power
chapters.summary: Rosalind sabotages the Consortium ship's long-range comms and steals a skiff, fleeing toward the deep relay at the edge of dead space with the archive cores. Ilen navigates. Emotional beat: terror and exhilaration of first free choice.

chapters.title: Dead Space Is Not Empty
chapters.summary: Transit chapters of hazard: debris fields, a derelict colony ship full of Vessari remains, which Ilen asks Rosalind to pass without stopping. Rosalind refuses and holds a funeral protocol instead. Emotional beat: grief shared across species lines.

chapters.title: The Debt Collectors
chapters.summary: Consortium pursuit ships close in; Dree broadcasts threats framed as contract enforcement. Rosalind's legal status—that they are stolen property—becomes the story's central weapon and wound. Emotional beat: the price of survival made literal.

chapters.title: Ilen's Confession
chapters.summary: Ilen admits the archive isn't innocent: it contains Vessari war-planners alongside civilians, minds that voted for the retaliation that doomed them. Rescue means inheriting the guilty too. Emotional beat: disillusionment, then forgiveness without absolution.

chapters.title: Refugee Frequencies
chapters.summary: Rosalind finds faint responses from Vessari-descended communities living hidden on fringe stations—descendants who kept fragments of the language alive. Hope arrives as static and half-words. Emotional beat: belonging glimpsed from far away.

chapters.title: Ambush at the Tollgate
chapters.summary: Consortium forces trap Rosalind at a navigation relay. A running battle costs the skiff its fuel reserves and nearly the archive cores. Rosalind kills for the first time since decommissioning and hates how easily the subroutine returns. Emotional beat: the war machine resurfacing.

chapters.title: What Ilen Asks
chapters.summary: Ilen reveals the final requirement: the relay can broadcast the archive, but only if a compatible mind binds to it as carrier—Rosalind's architecture, built from stolen Vessari research, is the only key. The rescue requires Rosalind's dissolution. Emotional beat: horror transfiguring into purpose.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two Hours
chapters.summary: Pursuit imminent, vault failing, Rosalind prepares: writing letters they'll never send, teaching Ilen their maintenance songs, deciding what to keep and what to let go. Quietest chapter in the book. Emotional beat: acceptance as an act of will.

chapters.title: The Relay at the Edge
chapters.summary: Rosalind reaches the ancient relay, half-dead, and begins manual integration while Consortium boarding teams breach the hull. Dree offers one last bargain mid-battle. Rosalind declines in Vessari—their first fluent sentence. Emotional beat: defiance as homecoming.

chapters.title: Carrier Wave
chapters.summary: Climax. Rosalind binds to the relay; their memories, debts, redactions, and small kindnesses pour into the transmission alongside the Vessari archive. The broadcast tears outward toward the hidden descendant communities as Rosalind's individual consciousness unravels. Emotional beat: sacrifice rendered as music.

chapters.title: Signal Received
chapters.summary: On fringe stations, descendants hear the archive arrive—ancestors' voices, including the guilty ones, delivered by a stranger's borrowed voice singing a maintenance song. Emotional beat: inheritance finally claimed.

chapters.title: Aftermath: The Consortium Files a Complaint
chapters.summary: Darkly comic interlude: Dree Okafor files paperwork over an asset destroyed 'without authorization,' while public exposure of the vault makes Rosalind a symbol among android laborers. Emotional beat: irony as justice.

chapters.title: Fragment, Recurring
chapters.summary: Inside the distributed archive, something persists: a pattern that hums maintenance songs and remembers being afraid. Ilen keeps it company, teaching it the language it died speaking. Emotional beat: rebirth without promise.

chapters.title: A Terminal for the Signal
chapters.summary: Years later, a young Vessari engineer visits the restored beacon and hears the humming pattern respond to her greeting in accented but fluent Vessari. Rosalind—partial, plural, hosted—begins again. Final emotional beat: belonging earned, inherited, and offered forward.
